questions.q: What is the real production risk of leaving max server memory at its default, per this lesson?
options: The buffer pool can grow until it starves the OS and other processes of memory, a common cause of an unexplained sudden slowdown
The database will refuse to start
There is no risk — the default is always safe
It only affects tempdb, not the buffer pool
questions.explain: Left unlimited, SQL Server can consume enough memory to starve the OS and any other software on the box.

questions.q: What does optimize for ad hoc workloads actually change about plan caching?
options: It caches only a small stub plan on a query's first execution, only promoting to a full cached plan if that exact query text runs a second time
It disables the plan cache entirely
It forces every query to use the same plan
It has no effect on plan caching at all
questions.explain: This setting specifically reduces plan cache bloat from one-off ad hoc queries that will never run again.

questions.q: Why does this lesson insist the configuration review is not a checklist to copy onto every server with the same numbers?
options: Every option has a real tradeoff, and the right value depends on the specific workload and hardware
sp_configure settings are randomized per server
Configuration options can only be set once per SQL Server version
There is only ever one correct value for every option
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this as a deliberate review requiring understanding of why a value fits a given workload, not a universal template.

questions.q: What must you run before most advanced sp_configure options become visible?
options: EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE;
DBCC CHECKDB
ALTER DATABASE ... SET RECOVERY FULL
sp_add_job
questions.explain: Most performance-relevant sp_configure options are hidden as 'advanced' until this switch is enabled.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a correctly-tuned setting with no documented reasoning is just as risky as an untouched default?
options: The next DBA (or the same one, months later) has no way to know if the non-default value is still appropriate for current conditions
Documentation is a compliance requirement, not a practical concern
Undocumented settings automatically revert to default
There's no real risk either way
questions.explain: Without documented reasoning, nobody can tell later whether a deliberate choice still makes sense as the workload or hardware changes.
